case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an ERISA imprudent-investment claim based on alleged fund underperformance must plead a “meaningful benchmark” to plausibly allege that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently under the circumstances.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA § 404(a)(1) (29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)) duty of prudence (care, skill, prudence, and diligence) and related fiduciary obligations; also implicated in the record are Article III standing principles and ERISA disclosure provisions (e.g., ERISA § 104(b)(4), 29 U.S.C. § 1024(b)(4)) though the cert petition’s question focuses on prudence pleading standards.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that for underperformance-based imprudence claims, ERISA plaintiffs should not be required at the pleading stage to identify a “meaningful benchmark” (or at least not in the strict manner applied by some courts) and that alleging the fiduciary failed to act with ERISA’s required care, skill, prudence, and diligence—together with allegations of underperformance and other circumstantial facts—should suffice to proceed to discovery.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that established ERISA pleading principles require plaintiffs challenging investment performance to allege a sound basis for comparison—i.e., a meaningful benchmark—because without it the complaint cannot plausibly show that a prudent fiduciary would have made a different decision; they also contend this case is factbound and a poor cert vehicle given its atypical investment strategy (risk-mitigation using alternative assets like hedge funds/private equity) and other issues (including standing/disclosure disputes in the broader litigation), and that the Ninth Circuit correctly affirmed dismissal.
key_precedents: Meiners v. Wells Fargo & Co., 898 F.3d 820 (8th Cir. 2018)
Thole v. U.S. Bank N.A., 140 S. Ct. 1615 (2020)
Virginia Military Institute v. United States, 508 U.S. 946 (1993)
Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C., 541 U.S. 913 (2004)
Magadia v. Wal-Mart Associates, Inc., 999 F.3d 668 (9th Cir. 2021)
Strubel v. Comenity Bank, 842 F.3d 181 (2d Cir. 2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Barrett’s strongest point—that § 1104(a)(1)(B) itself is comparative (“like character” and “like aims”)—is well taken, and it justifies demanding nonconclusory allegations establishing meaningful comparability under Twombly/Iqbal; a bare “we underperformed” claim cannot proceed. But I remain concerned that the Eighth Circuit’s benchmark-centric formulations, even if not intended as “magic words,” function in application as a categorical screen, in tension with Hughes and Dudenhoeffer’s insistence on careful, context-sensitive scrutiny rather than rigid pleading prerequisites. The minimal, legitimacy-preserving course is to vacate and remand with guidance that comparators (whether a benchmark or functionally equivalent allegations) will often be necessary, yet courts must not foreclose other concrete allegations that plausibly establish like aims and imprudence under the circumstances then prevailing. That approach gives full effect to the statutory comparative frame while avoiding an across-the-board rule that our recent ERISA pleading precedents caution against.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s remand proposal, echoed by Justice Kagan, is the strongest counter: Hughes and Dudenhoeffer caution against turning a “meaningful benchmark” into a categorical, magic-words prerequisite. But that concern does not undermine my position because § 1104(a)(1)(B) itself supplies the comparative frame (“enterprise of a like character and with like aims”), so insisting on some nonconclusory like-for-like factual basis is not an extra-textual screen—it is what makes an underperformance inference plausible under Twombly/Iqbal and Dudenhoeffer’s anti-hindsight logic. Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry point is weighty, yet it cannot displace Rule 8’s demand for factual content where the statute makes comparability central to the duty’s original public meaning. Properly understood, Hughes rejects rigid labels, not the statutory requirement that a prudence claim plead facts tethering “underperformance” to comparable aims, risks, and strategies.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point seriously: Hughes and Dudenhoeffer warn against rigid, categorical pleading screens and certainly do not require plaintiffs to recite a “meaningful benchmark” label. But Justice Thomas is right that § 1104(a)(1)(B) itself makes prudence a comparative inquiry (“like character and with like aims”), so in an underperformance-only theory the complaint must plead some nonconclusory like-for-like basis (or functionally equivalent facts establishing comparable aims/risk/strategy) to make imprudence plausible under Twombly/Iqbal rather than mere hindsight disagreement. Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry concern cannot justify allowing discovery on indeterminate allegations that any lag equals imprudence when the statutory standard is relational and demands facts showing the comparison is apt. Roberts’s remand approach is attractive as a matter of phrasing, but unless we clearly require a coherent comparative foundation, lower courts will effectively permit outcome-based suits untethered to “like aims,” undermining Dudenhoeffer’s gatekeeping function and imposing undue discovery costs on fiduciaries.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that §1104(a)(1)(B) speaks in comparative terms (“like character” and “like aims”)—is real, and it justifies demanding nonconclusory allegations that make any comparison intelligible under Twombly/Iqbal. But I agree with Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice that Hughes and Dudenhoeffer reject turning one probative way of doing that (a named “meaningful benchmark”) into an across-the-board pleading prerequisite that can bar other concrete allegations of an imprudent process when fiduciaries hold the key information. The respondent-side approach risks functionally insulating sustained, plausibly explained underperformance coupled with process red flags unless participants can identify a court-approved comparator at the outset, which conflicts with ERISA’s remedial purpose and access-to-justice realities. The proper course is to vacate and remand for context-sensitive plausibility review that polices comparability rigorously when plaintiffs rely on it, but does not mandate a single comparator form in every underperformance theory.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is textual: § 1104(a)(1)(B) speaks in relational terms (“like character” and “like aims”), so a complaint must supply some nonconclusory basis for comparability to distinguish imprudence from different risk/strategy choices. But that does not entail, as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett’s approach risks in application, a de facto categorical requirement that plaintiffs plead a specific “meaningful benchmark” in every underperformance-only case; Hughes and Dudenhoeffer’s insistence on “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” counsels against hard-wiring one evidentiary form into Rule 8. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Twombly/Iqbal can—and should—screen out bare “we underperformed” allegations, while still permitting plausibility to be shown through functionally equivalent factual matter (plan objectives, constraints, fees, magnitude/duration of lag, and process indicia) that effectively establish “like aims” without a single named index. On pragmatic textualist grounds, the statute demands comparability, but it does not dictate a single pleading format, and our precedent warns against turning helpful comparators into rigid gatekeeping rules.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice offer the strongest pushback: Hughes and Dudenhoeffer caution against rigid, categorical pleading screens, and I agree we should not impose a magic-words “meaningful benchmark” requirement. But Justice Thomas’s textual point remains decisive under my methodology: §1104(a)(1)(B) defines prudence by reference to an “enterprise of a like character and with like aims,” so an underperformance-only theory must plead nonconclusory facts establishing like-for-like comparability (whether styled as a benchmark or equivalent allegations about aims, risk, and strategy) to satisfy Twombly/Iqbal as applied in Dudenhoeffer. The Roberts/Kagan remand approach is attractive in tone, yet without a clear insistence on the statute’s comparative frame it risks authorizing discovery based on outcome dissatisfaction untethered to “like aims,” inviting hindsight litigation that ERISA’s text and our plausibility precedents do not permit. Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry concern is real, but it cannot relax Rule 8 where the statutory standard itself makes comparability the linchpin for inferring imprudence rather than different lawful risk choices.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the strongest point that Hughes and Dudenhoeffer caution against turning a “meaningful benchmark” into a rigid, talismanic pleading prerequisite, and I agree we should say explicitly that no magic words or single index is required. But Justice Thomas’s textual anchor—§ 1104(a)(1)(B)’s “enterprise of a like character and with like aims”—means an underperformance-only claim must still plead nonconclusory facts establishing a like-for-like basis (whether via a benchmark or functionally equivalent allegations) to make imprudence plausible under Twombly/Iqbal rather than mere disagreement with risk/strategy. The information-asymmetry concern raised by Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson is real, yet it cannot substitute for allegations that plausibly separate imprudence from different aims or constraints “under the circumstances then prevailing,” especially for complex investment approaches where raw performance comparisons are unreliable. On this record, dismissal should be affirmed while clarifying—consistent with Roberts/Kagan—that “benchmark” is not a categorical label, but comparability is an essential factual predicate for plausibility.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the strongest point that Hughes and Dudenhoeffer reject rigid, categorical pleading prerequisites, and I agree we should not enshrine “meaningful benchmark” as a magic-words rule. But Justice Thomas is right that § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s text (“enterprise of a like character and with like aims”) builds comparability into the prudence standard itself, so an underperformance-only theory must plead nonconclusory facts establishing a like-for-like basis (whether via a benchmark or functionally equivalent allegations) to make imprudence plausible under Twombly/Iqbal. Chief Justice Roberts’s remand approach is attractive in form, yet if it permits bare underperformance allegations without coherent comparability facts, it risks diluting the statutory comparative frame and inviting hindsight-driven discovery. On this record, insisting on some pleaded comparability is not an extra-textual gate but an application of the statute’s own relational standard in the “circumstances then prevailing.”

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is textual: § 1104(a)(1)(B) expressly measures prudence against an “enterprise of a like character and with like aims,” so comparability must do real work in separating imprudence from mere risk/strategy differences. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts (and Justice Kagan) that insisting on a single “benchmark” form at the pleadings stage risks becoming the very categorical gatekeeping Hughes and Dudenhoeffer reject; Twombly/Iqbal already permits dismissal of conclusory or inapt comparisons while leaving room for other concrete allegations that effectively establish “like aims” (fees, strategy mismatch, process red flags) where information is asymmetrically held by fiduciaries, as Justice Sotomayor notes. The respondent-side approach, as framed by Justices Barrett and Kavanaugh, is persuasive only insofar as it demands nonconclusory comparability facts—not if it hardens into a near-automatic dismissal rule whenever plaintiffs cannot name a court-approved comparator at Rule 12. On my pragmatic, procedural-fairness view, the proper disposition is to vacate and remand for context-sensitive plausibility review that enforces the statute’s comparative frame without converting “benchmark” into a mandatory pleading threshold.

John Roberts.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence is expressly “context specific,” turning on the “circumstances … prevailing” when the fiduciary acted, 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), and this Court has rejected categorical pleading rules that short-circuit that inquiry. In Dudenhoeffer and Hughes v. Nw. Univ., we required plausibility under Twombly/Iqbal but emphasized that courts must evaluate prudence allegations in a careful, circumstance-sensitive way, not by imposing an across-the-board prerequisite like a “meaningful benchmark” in every underperformance case. A benchmark may often be necessary to make underperformance allegations plausible, but making it an absolute pleading requirement risks converting a fact-intensive fiduciary inquiry into a rigid rule inconsistent with Hughes and undermines uniform ERISA administration. The narrower, institutionally cautious course is to vacate and require application of ordinary plausibility principles without a categorical benchmark mandate, leaving room for dismissal where the pleaded comparisons are inapt.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: ERISA’s text requires measuring fiduciary conduct against what a prudent person would do “in the conduct of an enterprise of a like character and with like aims,” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), which necessarily calls for some meaningful comparison to plausibly allege that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently. Under this Court’s Rule 12 framework in Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, complaints must contain nonconclusory allegations permitting a context-specific inference of imprudence, and a bare assertion of “underperformance” without a sound benchmark is typically too indeterminate to satisfy that standard. Requiring plaintiffs to plead a meaningful benchmark is not a categorical extra-textual hurdle but a common-sense application of plausibility to the statute’s “like character” comparator and the fiduciary’s circumstances. Absent such allegations, the complaint fails to connect performance outcomes to imprudent process in a way that makes breach plausible rather than speculative.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence is expressly tethered to “the circumstances then prevailing,” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), so a complaint alleging “underperformance” must supply a plausible, context-specific basis to infer that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently. Under Dudenhoeffer, courts must apply ordinary plausibility pleading to filter out conclusory allegations in prudence claims, and without a meaningful benchmark or comparator with similar objectives and risk profile, “underperformance” is not an informative metric and invites costly, intrusive discovery against plan fiduciaries. Hughes rejected categorical rules that dilute the context-specific inquiry, but requiring some coherent benchmark is not a rigid talisman; it is the minimum factual content needed to make the underperformance theory plausible. Practical consequences reinforce this: absent a benchmark requirement, fiduciaries (and thus plans and participants) bear heavy litigation costs and risk being second-guessed for legitimate risk-mitigation strategies.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence under § 404(a)(1)(B), 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), is explicitly “context specific,” and this Court has rejected categorical pleading rules that short-circuit that inquiry at the Rule 12 stage. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer requires “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny,” not a rigid comparator requirement, and Hughes v. Northwestern Univ. reiterates that categorical pleading rules are inconsistent with ERISA’s circumstances-prevailing standard. Requiring plaintiffs—often plan participants without access to detailed investment data pre-discovery—to plead a court-approved “meaningful benchmark” risks insulating imprudent conduct from review and undermines access to justice for vulnerable workers whose retirement security is at stake. Plausibility can be shown through underperformance plus surrounding allegations (fees, strategy mismatches, process failures) without turning “meaningful benchmark” into an absolute gatekeeping rule.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: ERISA § 404(a)(1)(B) makes prudence a circumstance-specific inquiry, and our cases caution against categorical pleading rules that short-circuit that context (Hughes v. Nw. Univ., 595 U.S. 170, 173 (2022)). Dudenhoeffer applies Twombly/Iqbal to require “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” and plausible allegations that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently, but it does not mandate any single form of factual showing—like a rigid “meaningful benchmark” requirement—in every underperformance case (573 U.S. 409, 425 (2014)). A benchmark will often be highly probative, but treating it as a pleading prerequisite risks turning a helpful evidentiary tool into a categorical rule inconsistent with ERISA’s text (“like aims” and “circumstances … prevailing”) and with workability given disclosure limits at the pleading stage. The better course is to allow complaints to proceed when they plausibly allege imprudence through concrete facts (including, where available, appropriate comparators), while leaving courts to police conclusory claims under Twombly/Iqbal case-by-case rather than by imposing a per se benchmark mandate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence is expressly comparative and context-dependent: it asks what “a prudent man acting in a like capacity . . . [in] an enterprise of a like character and with like aims” would do “under the circumstances then prevailing.” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B). Under Dudenhoeffer, Rule 12 demands “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” to ensure the complaint plausibly alleges that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently; in an underperformance theory, that plausibility ordinarily requires some non-conclusory basis for comparison—i.e., a meaningful benchmark—so the court can assess whether the alleged underperformance signals imprudence rather than differing risk, strategy, or aims. This is not a categorical extra-textual rule so much as the application of Twombly/Iqbal plausibility to a statute that itself frames prudence in relative, like-for-like terms, and it aligns with decisions such as Meiners requiring a “sound basis for comparison” to infer imprudence from returns and fees.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: ERISA § 404(a)(1)(B) requires a context-specific prudence inquiry, but under Twombly/Iqbal as applied in Dudenhoeffer, a complaint must plead sufficient factual content to make it plausible that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently under the circumstances. In an underperformance theory, some sound comparator is ordinarily necessary to move the allegation from “the fund did poorly” (which may reflect its strategy) to “the fiduciary acted imprudently,” and a meaningful benchmark is a practical, workable way to enforce that plausibility requirement without authorizing fishing-expedition discovery. Hughes cautions against rigid categorical rules, but it does not eliminate the need for a plausible factual basis; requiring a benchmark (or functionally equivalent factual allegations establishing comparability) is consistent with Dudenhoeffer’s demand for careful, context-sensitive pleading. Given the atypical alternative-asset, risk-mitigation strategy here, insisting on a comparator with similar objectives is especially important to avoid judging prudence with hindsight rather than the “circumstances…prevailing” at the time.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence is expressly comparative and contextual: the fiduciary must act as a prudent person “acting in a like capacity” in an “enterprise of a like character and with like aims.” 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B). Under Dudenhoeffer, courts must apply “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” at the Rule 12 stage to ensure the complaint plausibly alleges that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently, not merely that returns were disappointing. 573 U.S. 409, 425 (2014). In an underperformance theory, that plausibility ordinarily requires allegations identifying a sound basis for comparison—i.e., a meaningful benchmark—because without a like-for-like comparator (accounting for strategy, risk, fees, and objectives) the inference of imprudence is conclusory; this aligns with the approach reflected in Meiners v. Wells Fargo & Co., 898 F.3d 820 (8th Cir. 2018). Hughes v. Northwestern rejects rigid categorical pleading rules, 595 U.S. 170, 173 (2022), but it does not eliminate the need for factual content showing imprudence under the circumstances, which a meaningful benchmark typically supplies in underperformance cases.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence requires a “context specific” inquiry into “the circumstances … prevailing” when fiduciaries acted, 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B), and this Court has cautioned that categorical pleading rules are inconsistent with that framework. Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer, 573 U.S. 409, 425 (2014); Hughes v. Nw. Univ., 595 U.S. 170, 173 (2022). Requiring plaintiffs in all underperformance cases to plead a court-approved “meaningful benchmark” risks imposing an extra-textual, rigid threshold that can block potentially meritorious claims before discovery, undermining procedural fairness where key comparator information may be within fiduciaries’ control. At the pleading stage, Twombly/Iqbal plausibility can be satisfied through particularized allegations about fees, strategy, and sustained underperformance in the relevant market context without a mandatory benchmark label, leaving the merits to be tested on a fuller record.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether an ERISA imprudent-investment claim based on alleged fund underperformance must plead a “meaningful benchmark” to plausibly allege that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently under the circumstances.
case_analysis.legal_provision: ERISA § 404(a)(1) duty of prudence and related fiduciary duties, 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1) (and, per the record excerpts, ancillary provisions implicated in the case’s background include ERISA § 104(b)(4), 29 U.S.C. § 1024(b)(4), and Article III standing requirements under the U.S. Constitution).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that for imprudence claims predicated on underperformance, it should not be mandatory at the pleading stage to identify a specific “meaningful benchmark” (e.g., a particular index or peer group) to state a claim; alleging that the fiduciary failed to act with ERISA’s required “care, skill, prudence, or diligence” in selecting/maintaining the challenged investments should be sufficient to proceed, with details about appropriate comparators developed in discovery.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents contend the Ninth Circuit correctly required a sound basis for comparison—i.e., a meaningful benchmark—because without a plausible comparator plaintiffs cannot infer imprudence from underperformance; they emphasize ERISA evaluates prudence in context and at the portfolio level (including diversification and risk objectives), and argue the complaint relied on generalized attacks on hedge funds/private equity costs and risks without facts showing these specific investments were imprudent for the Plans’ risk-mitigation strategy; they also argue the case is a poor vehicle and does not warrant certiorari, contrasting it with Parker-Hannifin’s interlocutory posture and noting practical concerns (including potential recusal effects in the other case).
key_precedents: Meiners v. Wells Fargo & Co., 898 F.3d 820 (8th Cir. 2018)
Va. Mil. Inst. v. United States, 508 U.S. 946 (1993)
Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C., 541 U.S. 913 (2004)
Thole v. U.S. Bank N.A., 140 S. Ct. 1615 (2020)
Magadia v. Wal-Mart Assocs., Inc., 999 F.3d 668 (9th Cir. 2021)
Strubel v. Comenity Bank, 842 F.3d 181 (2d Cir. 2016)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest point: §1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing” language makes a bare “it underperformed” theory inherently comparative, and without risk/fee/objective context a complaint can devolve into hindsight. But Hughes and Dudenhoeffer—emphasized by Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch—counsel against converting that practical necessity into a categorical Rule 12 requirement to plead a particular “meaningful benchmark” in every case, which would harden a circuit gloss (Meiners) into an element and undermine our own insistence on context-sensitive scrutiny. The narrow, institutionally legitimate course is to reaffirm that comparative context is often essential to plausibility in underperformance claims while holding the Ninth Circuit erred insofar as it treated the absence of a specified benchmark as dispositive rather than assessing whether other concrete allegations supplied equivalent context. That approach respects the statutory text without announcing a rigid, judge-made pleading screen.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan offer the strongest opposing point: Hughes and Dudenhoeffer caution against rigid, judge-made “categorical” pleading screens. But that caution does not negate ERISA’s text, which asks whether a fiduciary acted prudently “under the circumstances then prevailing” and “acting in a like capacity”; an underperformance-only theory is inherently comparative, so Rule 8 plausibility ordinarily requires allegations supplying a like-for-like basis (often a benchmark, or equivalent facts about risk, strategy, and fees) rather than hindsight dissatisfaction. As Justice Alito explains, without that contextual comparator content, the inference that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently is speculative, and Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” directs courts to screen out such conjecture at the pleadings stage. Hughes rejected per se rules, not the ordinary application of plausibility to a claim whose premise depends on meaningful similarity in circumstances and capacity.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The strongest point on the other side, pressed by the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan, is that Hughes and Dudenhoeffer warn against rigid, categorical pleading screens; I agree we should not announce an index-by-name checklist as a universal element. But those cases still require “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny” under Rule 8, and §1104(a)(1)(B)’s text (“like capacity,” “circumstances then prevailing”) makes an underperformance-only theory inherently comparative—without a meaningful comparator or functional equivalent allegations controlling for risk, strategy, objectives, and fees, the inference of imprudence is speculative hindsight. Justice Sotomayor’s information-asymmetry concern is serious, yet it cannot justify discovery burdens where the complaint supplies no pleaded basis to infer that a prudent fiduciary would have chosen a genuinely like alternative. Properly understood, Meiners reflects ordinary plausibility application to this posture, not a judge-made heightened pleading rule, and the Ninth Circuit’s dismissal fits Dudenhoeffer’s directive to screen implausible claims at the pleadings stage.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett make the strongest textual point that §1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing” require some way to control for risk, strategy, and objectives, and I agree a comparator is often the most straightforward vehicle. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan explain, Hughes and Dudenhoeffer caution against converting that practical evidentiary need into a dispositive, across-the-board Rule 12 prerequisite—especially where “comparator-like” context can be pleaded through concrete facts about fees, stated objectives, and persistent lagging performance relative to readily available alternatives. Justice Alito’s discovery-cost concern is real, yet Rule 8 plausibility can be enforced without a judge-made “meaningful benchmark” element that, as Justice Jackson notes, would systematically disadvantage participants facing information asymmetry about fiduciary process and internal comparisons. On my pragmatic view of access to justice under ERISA, the better course is to reject a categorical benchmark requirement while insisting on context-sensitive scrutiny that demands nonconclusory, risk-and-objective-aware allegations.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that §1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing” language makes many underperformance theories inherently comparative, so a complaint must supply enough context—risk, strategy, fees, objectives—to make imprudence plausible. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Hughes and Dudenhoeffer forbid converting that practical necessity into a categorical Rule 12 requirement that plaintiffs must plead a named “meaningful benchmark” (or face automatic dismissal), which would effectively add a judge-made element untethered to ERISA’s text and Rule 8. I can accept Justice Alito’s discovery-cost concern while still insisting on a workable middle: courts should demand comparator-like factual content sufficient to permit a like-for-like inference, without hardening Meiners into an across-the-board pleading checklist. On that approach, comparator deficiencies can doom a complaint when they render allegations conclusory, but the absence of a particular benchmark should not be dispositive in every case.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s textual point about §1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing” language is forceful: underperformance theories are usually comparative, and complaints often must allege risk/fee/objective context to avoid hindsight. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Hughes and Dudenhoeffer forbid converting that practical need into a categorical Rule 12 prerequisite—nothing in ERISA’s text makes pleading a named “meaningful benchmark” an across-the-board element, as opposed to one common way to supply context. Justice Alito’s discovery-cost concern is answered by applying ordinary Rule 8 plausibility with “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny,” demanding nonconclusory allegations about strategy, fees, risks, and available alternatives, without elevating Meiners into a rigid gatekeeper rule. So I would reverse any rule treating the absence of a specified benchmark as dispositive while acknowledging that comparative allegations will frequently be necessary to make imprudence plausible.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s institutional point is the strongest for petitioner: Hughes and Dudenhoeffer counsel against rigid, categorical pleading screens, and I agree we should not constitutionalize an index-identification checklist. But Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett correctly anchor the analysis in §1104(a)(1)(B)’s text—“like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing”—which makes an underperformance-only theory inherently comparative; absent a pleaded benchmark or equivalent factual context controlling for risk/strategy/fees, the inference that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently remains speculative under ordinary Rule 8 plausibility as Dudenhoeffer applied it. Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s information-asymmetry concern is real, yet Hughes did not eliminate the need for context-sensitive scrutiny at the pleadings stage to prevent hindsight-based discovery fishing expeditions where the complaint itself supplies no like-for-like basis. Meiners is not binding, but it persuasively illustrates why, in this specific theory, comparator context is often indispensable to make imprudence plausible without converting Rule 12 into a merits trial.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice persuasively caution that Hughes and Dudenhoeffer disapprove categorical, judge-made pleading screens, and I agree we should not announce a formal rule that an index must be named in every case. But that does not answer the textual problem Justice Thomas and Justice Alito identify: § 1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing” make an underperformance-only theory inherently comparative, so a complaint must plead some nonconclusory comparator-like context (risk, strategy, fees, objectives, and plausible alternatives) to make imprudence more than hindsight. On this record, the Ninth Circuit’s insistence on a meaningful benchmark functions as an application of Rule 8 plausibility under Dudenhoeffer’s “careful, context-sensitive scrutiny,” not a heightened element; Hughes constrains per se rules, not the basic requirement that plaintiffs supply enough context for a like-for-like inference. Accordingly, I remain with Respondent even while accepting that courts should frame the standard as “sufficient comparative context,” not an inflexible benchmark checklist.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the strongest point for respondent: §1104(a)(1)(B)’s “like capacity” and “circumstances then prevailing” language makes underperformance theories inherently comparative and, in many cases, a benchmark (or functional equivalent) will be necessary to plead plausibility without hindsight. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that Hughes and Dudenhoeffer specifically warn against converting that practical reality into a categorical Rule 12 prerequisite that turns on the formal absence of a named “meaningful benchmark,” rather than on whether the complaint’s total factual context (fees, objectives, risk posture, persistent lag, available alternatives) plausibly alleges imprudence. Justice Alito’s discovery-cost concern does not justify a judge-made gate that systematically disadvantages plaintiffs where key comparator/process information is controlled by fiduciaries; Rule 8 plausibility plus case-management tools can screen conclusory claims without ossifying Meiners into an extra pleading element. On a progressive pragmatic view focused on procedural fairness and real-world access to adjudication, I would reaffirm “context-sensitive scrutiny” and reject any across-the-board benchmark requirement while leaving room for dismissal where the allegations truly lack comparative substance.

John Roberts.reasoning: ERISA’s duty of prudence under § 404(a)(1)(B) is “context specific” and turns on the “circumstances … prevailing” when the fiduciary acted, which counsels against a categorical pleading requirement that a complaint must always identify a particular “meaningful benchmark.” Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer and Hughes v. Northwestern reject rigid, across-the-board rules at the Rule 12 stage in favor of careful, case-by-case plausibility review, so courts can demand enough factual context to make imprudence plausible without mandating a specific comparator in every underperformance case. A mandatory benchmark rule risks converting pleading into a heightened requirement not found in ERISA or Rule 8, and can improperly insulate potentially imprudent conduct before discovery where relevant comparator information may be held by fiduciaries. A narrower course that preserves institutional legitimacy is to reaffirm Dudenhoeffer/Hughes: plaintiffs must plead facts that make it plausible a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently, and comparators may often be necessary, but they are not invariably required as a categorical matter.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: ERISA’s text requires judging prudence “under the circumstances then prevailing” and by reference to what a prudent fiduciary “acting in a like capacity” would do, 29 U.S.C. § 1104(a)(1)(B); an underperformance theory therefore must identify a sound comparator to make plausible the claim that a prudent fiduciary would have acted differently. Under Dudenhoeffer, a complaint must plead nonconclusory facts supporting that inference, and without a meaningful benchmark, allegations of “underperformance” are too context-free to satisfy Rule 12 plausibility. Hughes rejects rigid categorical pleading rules, but it does not relieve plaintiffs of alleging facts that make imprudence plausible in context; requiring some meaningful benchmark in an underperformance case is simply an application of that context-sensitive scrutiny. This approach also accords with Meiners v. Wells Fargo & Co., which held that “meaningful benchmark” allegations are necessary where imprudence is inferred from relative performance.
